concept.body: Why V = πr²h: a cylinder's cross-sections are constantly πr² (chapter 1), so it matches any prism of equal base area and height at every level, and Cavalieri (chapter 2) forces equal volumes — the prism's V = Bh transfers. The same argument prices ANY solid with constant sections: V = (section area)(length).

explanationVariants: Constant sections of area 12 along height 7.

commonErrors.feedback: 28 charges a third — that's for shrinking sections; constant pays full: 84.

steps.body: Grade 5 counted unit cubes into V = Bh for prisms. The cylinder inherits the formula by Cavalieri: stand it next to ANY prism with the same base AREA and height — every level of both shows that same area — so their volumes agree, and the cylinder's is Bh = πr²h. The formula Grade 8 recalled is now JUSTIFIED, not just remembered.

explanationVariants: Match the cylinder (base 25π) to a prism of base area 25π, height 8: every level shows 25π on both.

widget.prompt: A cylinder has radius 5 and height 8. Its Cavalieri twin is a prism with base area 25π and height 8. Both volumes' coefficient (of π) = ?

numericErrors.feedback: 40 = 5 × 8 forgets the square — the base is π(5²) = 25π: coefficient 200.
66.67 sneaks in a ⅓ — cylinders are prisms-in-spirit: full Bh = 200.

explanationVariants: Cavalieri's two clauses: same height, equal sections at every level.
The cylinder's constant circular sections make the second clause automatic.

options.label: Their equal-area sections match at every level.
options.feedback: Constancy (chapter 1's cylinder catalog) plus Cavalieri (chapter 2) — the course assembled this proof in pieces.

options.label: Circles are close enough to polygons.
options.feedback: Polygonal approximation is a valid alternative road, but the clean argument here is exact: constant equal sections + Cavalieri.

options.label: Every solid follows V = Bh.
options.feedback: Cones and spheres refuse Bh — the cylinder qualifies precisely BECAUSE its sections never change.

options.label: Their total surface areas are equal.
options.feedback: Surfaces differ and don't matter — Cavalieri reads slice areas only.

steps.body: A prism is its base, stacked.

widget.prompt: Move a horizontal section through the cylinder, then add a prism whose base has the same area. Test Cavalieri at several heights and finish at the middle slice.
widget.successFeedback: At every tested height, both solids expose the same cross-sectional area, and their heights match. Cavalieri therefore forces equal volumes—even though the base shapes and outer surfaces differ.
widget.positionFeedback: Keep testing sections, then place the section plane at the middle height to complete the comparison.
widget.comparisonFeedback: Add the equal-base-area prism. Cavalieri is a comparison theorem, so matching sections must be visible in both solids.
widget.invariantFeedback: Move the plane through several heights. One snapshot is not enough to establish that the section area stays constant.

predict.prompt: A cylinder and a prism have equal heights and equal base areas. What must match at every horizontal level?
predict.reveal: Cavalieri compares area slice by slice. Equal cross-sectional area at every height implies equal volume.

cml.actionGoal: Move a section plane and compare cross-sectional areas of two solids at matching heights.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: Replace the cylinder with a cone of the same base and height. Which section invariant breaks as the plane rises?

explanation.prompt: Why may the comparison prism have a differently shaped base?

options.label: Cavalieri needs equal cross-sectional area at each height, not matching outlines.
options.feedback: Exactly—area, not section shape or perimeter, is the load-bearing invariant.

options.label: The lateral surfaces are automatically equal.
options.feedback: Lateral surface area is unrelated to the slice-by-slice volume proof.

options.label: All prisms and cylinders have the same volume formula by definition.
options.feedback: The formula is justified by the equal-section argument, not by naming.

widget.prompt: To justify a cylinder's volume with Cavalieri, the comparison prism must have:

options.label: The same height and the same base area.
options.feedback: Any base shape works — square, triangle, blob — as long as its area is πr²; sections then match at every level.

options.label: A square base with side length r.
options.feedback: That base area is r², not πr² — the sections would run π-to-1 forever. Equal AREA is the requirement.

options.label: The same lateral surface area.
options.feedback: Surfaces don't testify — the twin needs equal base area and height.

options.label: A circular base with radius 2r.
options.feedback: That quadruples the section — the twin must MATCH πr², whatever its shape.

hints: The tunnel's cross-section is constant along its 50-length — a generalized cylinder (prism with a curvy base).
The justified rule for constant sections: V = (section area)(length).
Section area 18 given — no π, no decomposition needed.
explanationVariants: Constant sections of area 18 along length 50: V = 900 by the very argument that priced the cylinder.

widget.prompt: A tunnel's cross-section is a constant curvy shape of area 18 m², and the tunnel runs 50 m. Its volume = ?

numericErrors.feedback: 300 sneaks a ⅓ — thirds belong to shrinking sections (cones); constant ones pay full: 900.
450 halves — the full run of constant 18-slices: 900.

widget.explorationFeedback: Inspect the required exact-number states before checking.
widget.fallbackFeedback: V = 18 × 50 = 900 m³ — 'cylinder' was never about circles; it's about CONSTANT sections.
widget.successFeedback: V = 18 × 50 = 900 m³ — 'cylinder' was never about circles; it's about CONSTANT sections.

takeaways: Cylinder volume = Bh, justified: constant sections + Cavalieri against any equal-base prism.
The argument covers oblique cylinders and ANY constant-section solid (tunnels, troughs).
Half or partial sections scale the price by their ratio.
